passages.source_text: ἀλλὰ πᾶσαι μὲν ἀνεῴχθωσαν αὐτῷ θύραι, πάντες δὲ μοχθηροὶ καὶ θετοὶ λυέσθωσαν νόμοι, ζηλοτύποις ἀνθρώποις κείμενοι, οἵτινες ὑπὸ ἀνοίας κρατούμενοι καὶ τὸ εὔλογον νοεῖν μὴ βουλόμενοι, προσέτι δὲ καὶ τοὺς λεγομένους μοιχοὺς ὑφορώμενοι, ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Διὸς διά γε τοῦ Μίνωος καὶ τοῦ Ῥαδαμάνθυος εὐλόγως θετοῖς παίζονται νόμοις. Ἔρωτα γὰρ ἐπιδημήσαντα ψυχαῖς οὐκ ἔστιν ἐπισχεῖν. οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν ἑκούσιον τὸ τῶν ἐρώντων πάθος. αὐτίκα γοῦν ὁ Ζεὺς αὐτὸς ὁ τούτων, νομοθέτης μυρίαις συνῆλθεν γυναιξίν, καὶ ὑπ’ ἐνίων μὲν σοφῶν ἀνδρῶν εὐεργέτης πρὸς τεκνοποιίαν αἰνεῖται τὴν αὐτοῦ μίξιν ἀνθρώποις δωρούμενος, παρ’ οἷς δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ χάριτι ἠπίστατο ἀγνοούμενος, μετεμορφοῦτο τὴν ἰδέαν, ἵνα μήτε αὐτοὺς λυπῇ μήτε τοῖς ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ τεθεῖσιν νόμοις ἀντιπράττειν δοκῇ. δεῖ οὖν τῇ φιλοσοφίᾳ προσανέχουσαν καλοῦ βίου χάριν μιμεῖσθαι τοὺς ὁμολογουμένους κρείττονας, ὧν αἱ μίξεις μυρίαι γεγόνασιν.

καὶ ὑπὲρ τοῦ μὴ τὸν χρόνον παραναλίσκειν μάτην εἰς τὰς ἀποδείξεις τὰς πλείονας, ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Διὸς τοῦ πατρὸς θεῶν τε καὶ ἀνθρώπων ἄρξομαι τὰς ἐνίων μηνύειν κοινωνίας· πασῶν γὰρ ὑπομνησθῆναι διὰ τὸ πλῆθος ἀδύνατον. ἄκουε τοίνυν αὐτοῦ τοῦ μεγάλου Διὸς διὰ τὴν τῶν ἀνοήτων ἀνδρῶν ζηλοτυπίαν τὰς διὰ τῆς μεταμορφώσεως λανθανούσας κοινωνίας. ἐν πρώτοις γὰρ τῆς διαφόρου μίξεως τὴν ὑπονοουμένην τῆς μοιχείας ἁμαρτίαν σοφοῖς λῦσαι θέλων, ὁπότε ἔμελλεν γαμεῖν καὶ ὡς ἐπὶ πρώτῃ εὐνῇ κατὰ τοὺς πολλοὺς μοιχὸς εἰδὼς οὐ γινόμενος, διὰ τῆς δοκούσης (ὡς ἔφην) ἁμαρτίας τὸν ἀναμάρτητον γάμον ἐπορίσατο. ἀδελφὴν γὰρ αὐτοῦ Ἥραν οὖσαν γαμεῖ, ὁμοιωθεὶς κόκκυγος πτερῷ, ἐξ ἧς Ἥβη τε καὶ Εἰλείθυια ἐγένετο. τὴν Μῆτιν γὰρ χωρὶς τῆς πρὸς τινὰ μίξεως ἀποκυΐσκει, ὡς καὶ Ἥρα τὸν Ἥφαιστον.

ἔτι δὲ μίγνυται ἀδελφῇ τῇ ἐξ Οὐρανοῦ καὶ Θαλάσσης αὐτῷ γενομένῃ ἀπὸ τῆς Κρόνου ἐκτομῆς, . . . . Ἔρως καὶ Κύπρις, ἣν καὶ Διδώνην λέγουσιν. μίγνυται δὲ καὶ Ἀντιόπῃ τῇ Νυκτέως, σατύρῳ παρεικασμένος, ἐξ ἧς Ἀμφίων καὶ Ζῆθος γεγόνασιν. Ἀλκμήνῃ τε τῇ Ἀμφιτρύωνος γυναικὶ συνέρχεται, ὁμοιωθεὶς Ἀμφιτρύωνι τῷ γεγαμηκότι, ἐξ ἧς Ἡρακλῆς ἐγένετο. καὶ Αἰγίνῃ τῇ Ἀσωποῦ πλησιάζει, γενόμενος ἀετός, ἐξ ἧς Αἰακὸς τίκτεται. Ἀμαλθείᾳ δὲ τῇ Φώκου ὁμοιωθεὶς ἄρκτῳ συνευνάζεται. καὶ Δανάῃ τῇ Ἀκρισίου χρυσὸς ἐπερρύη, ἐξ ἧς Περσεὺς ἀνέπτη. Καλλιστοῖ τῇ Λυκάονος ἠγριώθη λέων, καὶ ἄλλον τίκτει Ἀρκάδα. Εὐρώπῃ τῇ Φοίνικος διὰ ταύρου συνῆλθεν, ἐξ ἧς Μίνως καὶ Ῥαδάμανθυς καὶ Σαρπηδὼν ἐξέφυσαν. Εὐρυμεδούσῃ τῇ Ἀχελῴου μύρμηξ γενόμενος, ἐξ ἧς Μυρμιδών. Ἑρσαίου νύμφῃ γενόμενος γύψ, ἐξ ἧς οἱ ἐν Σικελίᾳ Παλικοί. Ἱμαλίᾳ τῇ γηγενεῖ ἐν Ῥόδῳ διὰ ὄμβρου συνῆλθεν, ἐξ ἧς Σπαρταῖος, Κρόνιος, Κῦτος. Κασσιέπειαν ἐνύμφευσεν, ὁμοιωθεὶς τῷ γήμαντι Φοίνικι, ἐξ ἧς Ἀτύμνιος αὐτῷ ἐξέφυ. Νεμέσει τῇ Θεστίου, τῇ καὶ Λήδᾳ νομισθείσῃ, κύκνος ἢ χὴν γενόμενος Ἑλένην ἐτεκνώσατο, καὶ αὖθις ἀστὴρ γενόμενος Κάστορα καὶ Πολυδεύκην ἐξέφηνεν. Λαμίᾳ ἐπεμορφώθη ἔποψ.

Μνημοσύνην, αὐτὸς εἰκασθεὶς ποιμένι, Μουσῶν ἀποφαίνει μητέρα. Σεμέλην τὴν Κάδμου πυρσέων γαμεῖ, ἐξ ἧς Διόνυσον τελεῖ. Περσεφόνην αὐτὸς ἐκνυμφεύει τὴν θυγατέρα, αὐτὸς ὁμοιωθεὶς δράκοντι, τῇ καὶ γυναικὶ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ αὐτοῦ Πλούτωνος εἶναι νομισθείσῃ. καὶ ἄλλαις πολλαῖς καὶ δίχα μεταμορφώσεως μίγνυται, ζῆλον τῶν ἀνδρῶν οὐκ ἐχόντων ὡς ἐφ’ ἁμαρτίᾳ, ἀλλ’ εὖ εἰδότων ὅτι ἀφθόνως ταῖς γυναιξὶν αὐτῶν κοινωνῶν γεννᾷ, χαριζόμενος αὐτοῖς Ἑρμεῖς, Ἀπόλλωνας, Διονύσους, Ἐνδυμίωνας καὶ ὅσους ἄλλους εἰρήκαμεν, ἐκ μίξεως αὐτοῦ κάλλει διαπρεπεστάτους.

καὶ ἵνα μὴ εἰς ἄπειρον ἐξήγησιν τὸν χρόνον δαπανῶ, πάντων μετὰ Διὸς θεῶν ἀφθόνους εὑρήσεις κοινωνίας, οἱ ἀνόητοι δὲ μοιχείας λέγουσιν τῶν θεῶν, μηδὲ τῶν ἀρρένων τὰς μίξεις φυλασσομένων ὡς αἰσχράς, ἀλλὰ ἐπιτηδευόντων καὶ τοῦτο ὡς εὐπρεπές. αὐτίκα γοῦν αὐτὸς ὁ Ζεὺς Γανυμήδους ἐρᾷ, Ποσειδῶν Πέλοπος, Ἀπόλλων Κινύρου, Ζακύνθου, Ὑακίνθου, Φόρβαντος, Ὕλα, Ἀδμήτου, Κυπαρίσσου, Ἀμύκλα, Τρωΐλου, Βράγχου, Ἀτυμνίου, Πάρου, Ποτνιέως, Ὀρφέως — Διόνυσος δὲ Ἀδώνιδος, Ἀμπέλου, Ὑμεναίου, Ἑρμαφροδίτου, Ἀχιλλέως — ὁ δὲ Ἀσκληπιὸς Ἱππολύτου — καὶ Ἥφαιστος Πηλέως — Πὰν δὲ Δάφνιδος — ὁ δὲ Ἑρμῆς Περσέως, Χρύσου, Θέρσου, Ὀδρύσου — Ἡρακλῆς δὲ Ἀβδήρου, Δρύοπος, Ἰοκάστου, Φιλοκτήτου, Ἴλα, Πολυφήμου, Αἵμονος, Διόμου, Πειριθόου.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: But let every door be opened to him, and let all wicked and imposed laws laid down for jealous people be annulled. Such people, controlled by folly and unwilling to understand what is reasonable, while also looking suspiciously upon those called adulterers, are appropriately made sport of by Zeus himself, through Minos and Rhadamanthus, with enacted laws. For when Eros has come to dwell in souls, it is impossible to restrain him, since the passion of lovers is not voluntary. Indeed, Zeus himself, the lawgiver of these laws, had intercourse with countless women. Some wise men praise him as a benefactor toward procreation, because he grants human beings intercourse with himself; but among those by whom he knew himself to be unrecognized with respect to the favor, he transformed his appearance, so that he might neither distress them nor appear to act against the laws established by himself. Therefore, one who devotes herself to philosophy for the sake of a noble life must imitate those acknowledged to be superior, whose couplings have been countless.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάντες δὲ μοχθηροὶ καὶ θετοὶ λυέσθωσαν νόμοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: let all wicked and imposed laws ... be annulled
lexical_decisions.rationale: θετός denotes a law laid down or enacted, in contrast to what is natural; “imposed” retains that force.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Διὸς διά γε τοῦ Μίνωος καὶ τοῦ Ῥαδαμάνθυος εὐλόγως θετοῖς παίζονται νόμοις
lexical_decisions.chosen: are appropriately made sport of by Zeus himself, through Minos and Rhadamanthus, with enacted laws
lexical_decisions.rationale: Zeus is the agent, Minos and Rhadamanthus are intermediaries, and the dative νόμοις supplies the means; εὐλόγως may qualify either the mockery or the enactment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when Eros has come to dwell in souls
lexical_decisions.rationale: The personal name and participle preserve the image of Eros arriving and taking up residence rather than reducing it to an abstract feeling.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: παρ’ οἷς δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ χάριτι ἠπίστατο ἀγνοούμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: but among those by whom he knew himself to be unrecognized with respect to the favor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction is compressed. χάριτι may denote his favor, especially the sexual favor just mentioned, while ἀγνοούμενος says that he was unrecognized; “not favorably recognized” or “not welcomed for the favor” are also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: one who devotes herself to philosophy
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle is feminine singular; the English explicitly preserves the otherwise implicit female referent.

passages.text: And so that I may not waste time in vain on the more numerous demonstrations, I shall begin with Zeus himself, the father of gods and human beings, and disclose some of his unions, for it is impossible to recall them all because of their multitude. Listen, then, to the unions of great Zeus himself that remained hidden through transformation because of the jealousy of foolish men. For first, wishing to resolve for the wise the suspected sin of adultery in varied intercourse, when he was about to marry, he knew that although most people would regard him as an adulterer at the first bedding, he was not becoming one; and through the apparent sin, as I said, he procured a sinless marriage. For he marries Hera, who is his sister, after being made like a cuckoo in plumage, and from her Hebe and Eileithyia came into being. For he gives birth to Metis without intercourse with anyone, just as Hera also gives birth to Hephaestus.

lexical_decisions.chosen: disclose some of his unions
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνίων is taken partitively in light of the following contrast with all of the unions.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς διὰ τῆς μεταμορφώσεως λανθανούσας κοινωνίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: the unions ... that remained hidden through transformation
lexical_decisions.rationale: λανθάνω emphasizes escaping notice, while μεταμόρφωσις supplies the means of concealment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in varied intercourse
lexical_decisions.rationale: διάφορος can mean diverse or different; “intercourse with another” is a possible alternative, but the surrounding catalogue favors repeated intercourse in differing forms.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς ἐπὶ πρώτῃ εὐνῇ κατὰ τοὺς πολλοὺς μοιχὸς εἰδὼς οὐ γινόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: he knew that although most people would regard him as an adulterer at the first bedding, he was not becoming one
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negation is retained with γινόμενος. κατὰ τοὺς πολλούς is understood as marking popular judgment rather than the narrator’s own conclusion.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after being made like a cuckoo in plumage
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally the comparison is to a cuckoo’s wing or feather; “in plumage” expresses the respect in which the likeness is asserted without replacing the cuckoo image.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he gives birth to Metis
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀποκυΐσκω denotes bringing forth or giving birth, and the supplied object is explicitly Metis.

source_issues.source_quote: τὴν Μῆτιν γὰρ χωρὶς τῆς πρὸς τινὰ μίξεως ἀποκυΐσκει
source_issues.issue: The printed wording clearly names Metis as the one Zeus brings forth. This is mythographically unexpected, since a familiar account instead has Zeus bring forth Athena after swallowing Metis, but the supplied reading is intelligible and has therefore been translated without harmonization.

passages.text: Furthermore, he has intercourse with a sister of his who came into being from Uranus and Thalassa as a result of the cutting performed by Cronus, . . . . Eros and Cypris, whom they also call Didone. He also has intercourse with Antiope daughter of Nycteus, taking the likeness of a satyr, and from her Amphion and Zethus came into being. He has relations with Alcmene, the wife of Amphitryon, after being made like Amphitryon, the man who had married her, and from her Heracles came into being. He approaches Aegina daughter of Asopus after becoming an eagle, and from her Aeacus is born. He lies with Amalthea daughter of Phocus after being made like a bear. He flowed over Danae daughter of Acrisius as gold, and from her Perseus flew up. For Callisto daughter of Lycaon he became a fierce lion, and she bears another Arcas. He had intercourse with Europa daughter of Phoenix by means of a bull, and from her Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Sarpedon sprang forth. For Eurymedusa daughter of Achelous he became an ant, and from her came Myrmidon. For the nymph of Hersaeus he became a vulture, and from her came the Palici in Sicily. He had intercourse with Himalia the earthborn on Rhodes by means of rain, and from her came Spartaeus, Cronius, and Cytus. He took Cassiepeia as a bride after being made like Phoenix, the man who had married her, and from her Atymnius sprang forth for him. For Nemesis daughter of Thestius, who was also thought to be Leda, he became a swan or a goose and fathered Helen; and again, after becoming a star, he brought Castor and Polydeuces to light. For Lamia he assumed the form of a hoopoe.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as a result of the cutting performed by Cronus
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording denotes Cronus’s act of cutting; this avoids the misleading implication that Cronus himself was castrated.

lexical_decisions.chosen: whom they also call Didone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The translation preserves the printed name Διδώνην rather than silently replacing it with the mythologically familiar Dione.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For Callisto daughter of Lycaon he became a fierce lion
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἠγριώθη conveys becoming wild or fierce, while λέων supplies the lion image.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for the nymph of Hersaeus
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive is rendered directly. The precise identity intended by the unfamiliar name is uncertain, so it is not replaced with a figure from another mythographic form.

lexical_decisions.chosen: He took Cassiepeia as a bride
lexical_decisions.rationale: The active verb can denote making someone a bride or giving her in marriage; the catalogue of Zeus’s unions and the following disguise support the contextual rendering “took ... as a bride.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: after becoming a star, he brought ... to light
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both the stellar transformation and the manifestation imagery of ἐκφαίνω.

source_issues.source_quote: ἀπὸ τῆς Κρόνου ἐκτομῆς, . . . . Ἔρως καὶ Κύπρις
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a lacuna of exactly four dots between the surviving clauses. Its content is unavailable; the English retains all four dots, and no restoration has been supplied. The wording after the gap consequently remains syntactically fragmentary.
The printed proper name is Didone, although Dione would be expected as an epithet or identification of Cypris in familiar mythographic wording. The printed form is retained in the translation.

passages.text: He himself assumes a shepherd’s likeness and makes Mnemosyne the mother of the Muses. He marries Semele daughter of Cadmus while blazing, and from her brings Dionysus to completion. He himself takes his own daughter Persephone as a bride, after being made like a serpent—she who was also believed to be the wife of his brother Pluto. He also has intercourse with many others even without transformation, since the husbands feel no jealousy as though over a sin, but know well that, by freely having intercourse with their wives, he begets children and bestows upon them Hermeses, Apollos, Dionysuses, Endymions, and however many others we have mentioned, all exceptionally distinguished in beauty as a result of intercourse with him.

lexical_decisions.chosen: makes Mnemosyne the mother of the Muses
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀποφαίνω can mean show, declare, or cause to appear; in this catalogue of unions, “makes ... the mother” conveys the resulting maternity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: while blazing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual form is understood from its transparent association with πυρσός, “firebrand” or “blaze,” without silently replacing the printed word.

lexical_decisions.chosen: from her brings Dionysus to completion
lexical_decisions.rationale: τελέω means complete or bring to fulfillment; the wording may allude to Dionysus’s completed gestation rather than merely using a generic verb for begetting.

lexical_decisions.chosen: He himself takes his own daughter Persephone as a bride
lexical_decisions.rationale: Although the active verb can mean give in marriage, the serpent transformation and surrounding list of Zeus’s unions support the reflexive contextual sense “takes ... as a bride.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: χαριζόμενος αὐτοῖς Ἑρμεῖς, Ἀπόλλωνας, Διονύσους, Ἐνδυμίωνας
lexical_decisions.chosen: bestows upon them Hermeses, Apollos, Dionysuses, Endymions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source deliberately uses plural forms of the names, presenting such beautiful offspring as repeated types; the plurals are preserved.

source_issues.issue: The printed form πυρσέων is morphologically unusual in this construction. It may be an uncontracted participial form associated with πυρσός, supporting the fire imagery used in the translation; alternatively, the text may reflect a defective writing of πυρσὸς ὤν, “being a firebrand.”
source_issues.proposed_reading: Σεμέλην τὴν Κάδμου πυρσὸς ὢν γαμεῖ (conjectural; not adopted)

passages.text: And so that I may not spend time on an endless exposition, you will find that all the gods, together with Zeus, have unstinting unions, which fools call adulteries of the gods. Even the male gods do not avoid such couplings as shameful, but practice this too as something seemly. Indeed, Zeus himself loves Ganymede; Poseidon loves Pelops; Apollo loves Cinyras, Zacynthus, Hyacinthus, Phorbas, Hylas, Admetus, Cyparissus, Amyclas, Troilus, Branchus, Atymnius, Paros, Potnieus, and Orpheus—Dionysus loves Adonis, Ampelus, Hymenaeus, Hermaphroditus, and Achilles—Asclepius loves Hippolytus—and Hephaestus loves Peleus—Pan loves Daphnis—Hermes loves Perseus, Chrysus, Thersus, and Odrysus—and Heracles loves Abderus, Dryops, Iocastus, Philoctetes, Ilas, Polyphemus, Haemon, Diomus, and Pirithous.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάντων μετὰ Διὸς θεῶν ἀφθόνους ... κοινωνίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: all the gods, together with Zeus, have unstinting unions
lexical_decisions.rationale: μετά with the genitive means “with,” and ἄφθονος conveys abundance or lack of restraint.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μηδὲ τῶν ἀρρένων τὰς μίξεις φυλασσομένων ὡς αἰσχράς
lexical_decisions.chosen: Even the male gods do not avoid such couplings as shameful
lexical_decisions.rationale: τῶν ἀρρένων is taken as the subject of the genitive participle. It can alternatively be attached to μίξεις as “couplings with males”; the following all-male catalogue makes the same-sex reference clear in either construction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀλλὰ ἐπιτηδευόντων καὶ τοῦτο ὡς εὐπρεπές
lexical_decisions.chosen: but practice this too as something seemly
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιτηδεύω denotes deliberately practicing or pursuing something, while εὐπρεπές contrasts what is seemly with what is shameful.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Ilas
lexical_decisions.rationale: The transliteration preserves the printed smooth-breathing form and distinguishes it from Ὕλα, rendered “Hylas,” earlier in the same list.

source_issues.issue: The printed form denotes Ilas and differs from the earlier Ὕλα, Hylas. Since Heracles is commonly associated with Hylas, the form may be a proper-name variant or a copying or printing error, but the selected reading is clear and has not been normalized.

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
